topic: The Binary Secret of the Tower of Hanoi
target_audience: High school students and early undergraduate computer science students

sections.title: The Puzzle Setup: Rules of the Game
sections.content: Introduce the Tower of Hanoi components: three vertical pegs and a stack of 'n' disks of different sizes. Explain the two core rules: 1. Only one disk can be moved at a time. 2. A larger disk can never be placed on top of a smaller disk. Establish the goal: move the entire stack to a different peg in the minimum number of moves.
sections.example: A curious robot named 'Alpha' is trying to move 3 golden pancakes from Peg A to Peg C without ever squashing a smaller pancake.

sections.title: Prerequisite: Binary Counting as a Pulse
sections.content: Visualize binary counting as a sequence of bits flipping. Explain that in a binary number, each position (bit) represents a power of 2. Show a 3-bit counter (000 to 111) and highlight which specific bit changes during each increment. Use a 'lightbulb' graphic where 'Off' is 0 and 'On' is 1.
sections.example: Sequence: 000 -> 001 (Bit 1 flips) -> 010 (Bit 1 and 2 flip) -> 011 (Bit 1 flips). Notice that Bit 1 flips every 1 step, Bit 2 every 2 steps, and Bit 3 every 4 steps.

sections.title: The Mapping: Disks as Bits
sections.content: Create a one-to-one mapping between the binary bits and the disks. Disk 1 (smallest) corresponds to the rightmost bit (2^0). Disk 2 corresponds to the second bit (2^1), and so on. Explain the 'Magic Rule': Whenever a bit in the binary counter changes its value (0 to 1 or 1 to 0), the corresponding disk must be moved.
sections.example: In a 3-disk game, counting from 0 to 7 in binary (000 to 111) provides the exact timing for every move. When the counter goes from 000 to 001, Bit 1 changes, so we move Disk 1.

sections.title: The Directional Logic: Where to Move?
sections.content: Explain the spatial logic using a cyclic movement pattern. For an odd number of disks: move the smallest disk in the cycle A -> C -> B -> A. For an even number: A -> B -> C -> A. All other disks move to the only available legal position. This ensures the binary 'flip' always results in a valid move.
sections.example: Graphic: A triangular path showing Pegs A, B, and C. When the binary counter hits '001', Disk 1 (the smallest) follows the arrow from A to C.

sections.title: Synthesis: Solving the 3-Disk Puzzle
sections.content: Walk through the full 7-step solution ($2^3 - 1$) by incrementing the binary counter. Show a split-screen: left side increments binary (001, 010, 011...), right side animates the corresponding disk move. Emphasize that the 'rightmost changed bit' always identifies the disk to be moved.
sections.example: At Step 4 (binary 100), the 3rd bit is the rightmost bit that changed from the previous state (011). Therefore, we move Disk 3 (the largest).

sections.title: Conclusion: The Power of 2^n - 1
sections.content: Summarize why binary counting is the perfect mathematical model for this recursive problem. Introduce the formula for total moves: $M = 2^n - 1$. Explain that the binary representation of the move number tells you exactly which disk is currently in motion.
sections.example: If you had 64 disks like the Monks in the original legend, the binary counter would reach a number with 64 ones, taking $2^{64}-1$ moves—roughly 585 billion years!
